title: The Necklace
text:
Mathilde Loisel was pretty and charming but married to a minor clerk in the Ministry of Education, and she felt she had been born for luxury. When her husband proudly brought home an invitation to a ministry ball, she wept because she had nothing to wear. He gave her the four hundred francs he had saved for a gun so she could buy a dress. Then she lamented that she had no jewels, so she borrowed a diamond necklace from her rich school friend, Madame Forestier.

At the ball she was a triumph. But when they got home, the necklace was gone. They searched everywhere and could not find it. Rather than confess to her friend, they found an identical necklace in a jeweler's shop for thirty-six thousand francs. Loisel spent his inheritance and borrowed the rest from moneylenders, and they returned it without a word.

Then came ten years of poverty. They dismissed their maid and moved to an attic. Mathilde scrubbed floors, carried water and haggled over every sou. Her husband worked evenings copying documents. Her hands grew red, her hair untidy, her looks gone.

When the last debt was paid, Mathilde met Madame Forestier on the Champs-Elysees, still young and lovely, and told her the whole story with some pride. Her friend was deeply moved and took her hands. "Oh, my poor Mathilde! But mine was paste. It was worth five hundred francs at most."
lesson: Pride that keeps you from telling a friend the truth can cost far more than the embarrassment of an honest word. Admit problems early.
people: Mathilde Loisel, her husband, Madame Forestier
source: Guy de Maupassant, The Necklace (La Parure, 1884)
